newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan rebels fall back in face of army thrust.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan rebels fall back in face of army thrust.

text.p: Sri Lanka's army has launched its biggest offensive this year against rebel-held territory in the north and so far met no resistance, military officials and news reports said on Wednesday.
Tamil separatists abandoned two camps ahead of the major Sri Lankan army offensive, a defence ministry spokesman said.
Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) offered little resistance to advancing ground troops while the air force and artillery took on known rebel targets, Brigadier Tissa Jayatunga told Reuters.
"Troops have advanced nine kilometers (six miles) into enemy territory clearing two abandoned LTTE camps," he said, declining to give further details.

The move towards Mannar, on the northwest coast, was launched from north-central Vavuniya, 220 km (140 miles) from Colombo, on Independence Day on Tuesday, said military officials in the north of the country and in the capital.
Navy boats patrolled the waters off Mannar to prevent rebels escaping by sea, they said.
The officials, who declined to be identified, said they had no information on the exact number of troops.
The Midweek Mirror newspaper said thousands of government soldiers were involved in the attack and the operation was the biggest this year.
The clandestine radio of the LTTE, monitored by Reuters, said 20,000 government troops were taking part in the offensive.
LTTE officials in Paris said their international spokesman, Lawrence Thilakar, was not immediately available for comment.
Some military officials said the army was trying to link the frontline town of Vavuniya and the town of Kilinochchi, 70 km (48 miles) to Vavuniya's north.
Other military officials said the army's aim was to open a supply route to isolated Mannar on the northwest coast after intelligence reports of a rebel build-up in the area.

Defence analysts said the army's real objective could be Kilinochchi, as part of its long-planned effort to open a supply route to the northern Jaffna peninsula and ultimately link Colombo with the entire northern part of the island.
The LTTE radio station said air and artillery strikes in the area had preceded the offensive, and spotter planes were seen circling the area. There were no reports of casualties.

Kilinochchi, a town that fell to the army last July, has been the focus of recent fighting between the two sides. Kilinochchi's only current supply route is a road linking it to Jaffna on the northern tip of the Indian Ocean island.
The government can supply Jaffna, the LTTE's main stronghold in the country until last year, only by air or sea.
Early last month, the LTTE launched an offensive against government forces in the north in a failed effort to block off the Jaffna-Kilinochchi road.

In three days of fighting starting on January 9, the government said it lost 160 soldiers while the LTTE said 140 of its fighters, including 78 women, had been killed. Both sides said their opponents had suffered higher death tolls.
The LTTE has waged war for a separate Tamil homeland in the country's north and east since 1983.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the conflict but the LTTE says the toll is much higher.
